one_liner: Intel's SIMD multi-buffer SHA/MD5/SM3 hashing library; beats single-buffer SHA-256 throughput when many independent buffers are in flight.
what_it_does: Hashes many independent messages at once on one core. You create a context manager, submit contexts with FIRST/UPDATE/LAST/ENTIRE flags, and collect finished contexts from submit() or flush() in whatever order they complete; the digests are standard SHA-1/SHA-256/SHA-512/MD5/SM3. A separate mh_sha256/mh_sha1 API offers a synchronous init/update/finalize interface for one buffer, but it computes a Multi-Hash tree digest that does not equal standard SHA-256. The library also ships AES-XTS/GCM/CBC and a rolling hash, but it has no HMAC, SHA-3 or BLAKE, and it is not an OpenSSL-style one-call SHA256().
how_it_is_fast: It uses multi-buffer SIMD hashing: each vector lane runs the SHA-256 compression function on a different message, giving 4 messages per pass with SSE/AVX, 8 with AVX2 and 16 with AVX-512, and an out-of-order job scheduler keeps the lanes filled. On CPUs with SHA extensions the manager switches to SHA-NI x1/x2 kernels when few lanes are busy (thresholds are 4 lanes on the SSE path and 6 on the AVX-512 path; a source comment says 'shani is faster than sse sha256_mb'). Multi-Hash applies the same lane trick to a single buffer: it interleaves the buffer word by word into 16 segments, hashes them in parallel, then hashes the concatenated segment digests (a two-level tree hash). The kernels are hand-written NASM/gas assembly, chosen at runtime by CPUID dispatch.
when_to_use: Storage, dedup or object-store pipelines that checksum many independent chunks or objects at the same time (Ceph and SPDK vendor it as a git submodule).
You can keep at least a lane-width of jobs in flight (4 for SSE, 8 for AVX2, 16 for AVX-512) and can handle jobs completing out of order.
AVX-512 x86 servers that regularly have more than 6 SHA-256 jobs active at once. Below that the manager falls back to SHA-NI single-buffer code anyway.
Legacy MD5/SHA-1 checksumming of many streams, where the dependency chain leaves scalar code furthest behind (the whitepaper reports its largest gain, ~4.4x, for MD5 x8).
mh_sha256, only in a closed system such as dedup fingerprints where both producer and verifier use Multi-Hash and buffers are 1 KB or larger.
when_not_to_use: Hashing one stream at a time with submit-then-flush. Users measured it slower than OpenSSL: 3.36 s vs 2.48 s for 1 GB of SHA-256 (issue #111) and 466 vs 787 MB/s for single-buffer MD5 (issue #45). The maintainer's answer is to keep multiple jobs in flight.
You need a fast standard SHA-256 of one large buffer. mh_sha256 digests are not interoperable, and on x86 mh_sha256 dispatches only SSE/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 (no SHA-NI path).
Small messages with Multi-Hash. The whitepaper says the gains diminish for buffers below about 1 KB, and the maintainers say it needs blocks of about 1 KB.
macOS or Apple Silicon. They are not in CI (Linux x86-64/arm64/RISC-V and Windows are), and past issues report build failures on M1 (#86) and on macOS x86 (#88).
You need a certified or general-purpose crypto API. The README says it cannot achieve CMVP certification as a standalone module, and it has no HMAC, SHA-3 or BLAKE.

integration.form: static lib / shared lib (autotools, Makefile.unx, nmake on Windows; CMake experimental)
integration.dependencies: None at runtime beyond libc. The build needs NASM on x86-64 (gas on aarch64/RISC-V). OpenSSL is used only by the tests, perf harnesses and examples.
integration.min_toolchain: x86-64: NASM 2.14.01+ with GCC, Clang, ICC or MSVC 2019+. aarch64: gas 2.34+ and GCC 8+ (older gas needs --disable-sve2). RISC-V RVV: gas 2.39+ and GCC 12.1+.
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE4 minimum for SIMD paths; AVX/AVX2/AVX-512/SHA-NI chosen at runtime), aarch64 (crypto extensions, SVE2), RISC-V 64 (RVV), and a portable C base elsewhere. 32-bit x86 was removed in v2.26.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Managers and contexts are plain caller-owned structs with no internal locking, so use one manager per thread. Re-submitting a context that is still in flight returns ISAL_HASH_CTX_ERROR_ALREADY_PROCESSING.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — sha256_mb produces standard SHA-256 digests but needs an asynchronous submit/flush batching API and returns host-order uint32 words; mh_sha256 has a synchronous init/update/finalize API but produces a different, non-standard digest

gotchas: SHA-1/SHA-256 results come back as uint32 words in host order, so you must byte-swap them on little-endian to get the canonical digest, while MD5 comes back already byte-ordered (issue #121).

A context cannot be re-submitted until submit() or flush() hands it back, and contexts return out of order. Submitting LAST straight after FIRST without flushing looked like a wrong-hash bug to one user (#156). Redundant flush() calls are safe.

The manager must be 16-byte aligned (the tests use posix_memalign). A misaligned manager crashed the AVX2 flush under MSVC (#122). The mh_sha256 context is about 3.7 KB, and the header advises heap allocation.
Each submit/update call takes a uint32 length (under 4 GB per call). -flto needs -fno-strict-aliasing or tests can fail (#162, #165). The non-isal_-prefixed API has been deprecated since v2.25.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over BLAKE3 or KangarooTwelve when the digest must stay standard SHA-256/SHA-1/MD5 because of a fixed protocol or on-disk format, and you have many independent buffers to batch. If you control the hash choice and need one big buffer hashed fast, BLAKE3 or K12 fits better. The j-lanes and S-HASH entries describe the same multi-lane ideas as papers; this is Intel's maintained, shipping C/asm implementation, and sha256-simd is the Go-ecosystem counterpart.
verified_claims_summary: Intel's own July 2012 whitepaper reports that SHA256x4 Multi-Hash (a non-standard 4-segment tree mode) hashed a 1 MB buffer at about 5 cycles/byte on one core of a Sandy Bridge Core i7-2600 with Turbo off. That was about 2.6x faster than Intel's best single-buffer SHA-256 of the day (not OpenSSL), and MD5 x8 was about 4.4x faster. The paper gives no compiler, flags or code version, the shipped mh_sha256 uses 16 segments rather than 4, and nothing is published for the standard-digest sha256_mb or against SHA-NI hardware.
status_note: Actively maintained by Intel: v2.26.1 was released 2026-06-12, the last commit is 2026-07-23, and CI covers x86-64 Linux/Windows, arm64 and RISC-V. It is BSD-3-Clause and vendored by Ceph and SPDK, but it is an assembly-heavy built library rather than a file you can copy.
